read.title: The beat starts itself
text: Cardiac muscle does not need a nerve to start each beat. A few specialized cells contract weakly but depolarize on their own, because a slow leak of sodium drifts their membrane toward threshold. The fastest of them, in the sinoatrial (SA) node in the wall of the right atrium, reaches threshold first and so sets the pace for the whole heart.

From the SA node, the impulse spreads across both atria and along internodal pathways to the atrioventricular (AV) node. Here conduction slows for about a tenth of a second. That pause gives the atria time to finish pushing blood into the ventricles before the ventricles contract.

The impulse then travels down the AV bundle in the interventricular septum, splits into right and left bundle branches, and spreads through Purkinje fibers into the ventricular walls. Contraction begins at the apex and moves toward the base, squeezing blood up toward the arteries. Gap junctions in the intercalated discs pass the signal from cell to cell.

An electrocardiogram records these events from the skin. The P wave marks atrial depolarization, the QRS complex marks ventricular depolarization, and the T wave marks ventricular repolarization. Autonomic nerves change the rate but do not create the rhythm: the vagus nerve slows the SA node, and sympathetic nerves speed it up.
